title: The mouse
hook: a mountain of a god rides a mouse

segments.voice: Yesterday, the broken tusk, and a pen that couldn't stop. Your line was finish the thing. Did something get its last line? Today, look down, at Ganesha's feet. Day twenty-seven.

Here's a picture that makes children laugh. Ganesha: big belly, elephant head, four arms, sitting like a king. And under him, carrying the whole thing, a mouse. A tiny mouse, often looking up at him, sometimes nibbling a sweet. It makes no physical sense at all, and that's the point. In this tradition, gods have animals that carry them. Shiva rides Nandi, the bull. Vishnu rides Garuda, the great eagle. Durga rides a lion. Saraswati has her swan. Kartikeya, from the race, has his peacock. And the god of beginnings, the remover of obstacles, rides the smallest of them all. Today's word is the name for that animal.
screen: `A BIG GOD. A TINY MOUSE.` → `GODS HAVE THEIR RIDES.` → `THE SMALLEST OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Vahana. From a Sanskrit root, vah, to carry. A vahana is the one that carries: a vehicle, a mount. And a god's vahana isn't just transport. It tells you something about the god. People read the bull as strength and patience, the eagle as speed, the lion as courage. So why a mouse? Hindus give more than one answer, and it's worth hearing a few. One: a mouse gets into everything. Through walls, under doors, into the grain store. It finds a way in where nothing bigger could. That's what the remover of obstacles does. Two: the mouse is desire, restless, nibbling at everything, never satisfied. Ganesha sits on it. Not killing it. Riding it. Steering it. Wanting doesn't go away; it just stops being in charge. Three, and simplest: the huge is carried by the small. There are stories, too, about where the mouse came from. In some Puranas it's a being who was cursed, or a demon Ganesha defeated who became his mount. Those stories vary a lot, and no single one is the official answer. What the stories share is the picture. At Ganesh Chaturthi, the mouse sits at his feet in homes and street shrines, sometimes with its own little offering. And look at who is doing the lifting in that image. Not the god. The mouse. Small carries large. Every day. Quietly.
screen: `VAHANA — THE ONE THAT CARRIES.` · `THE MOUNT SAYS WHO THE GOD IS.` · `GETS IN ANYWHERE, OR RIDES DESIRE.` · `THE STORIES VARY.` · then, large: `SMALL CARRIES LARGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one small thing carrying something big. Sit and breathe. Look around you, or think back over today. What small thing is holding up something large? The chair under you. One bolt in a bridge. The person at the front desk. A single habit that keeps your week from falling apart. Pick one. Just look at it, and give it credit. The bell holds the time.
Vahana. The one that carries: the animal each god rides. Ganesha's is a mouse.
Your line: small carries large. Today, thank one small thing, or one quiet person, that carries a lot. Day twenty-seven.

howItsDone: In Hindu temples and home shrines a god's vahana often sits facing the deity; at Ganesh Chaturthi Ganesha's mouse is placed at his feet, sometimes with its own small offering.
